reverse_outline.summary: Part's three takeaways: one order record for all channels, connectors translate without owning, outside parties impose scores and deadlines
Same product sold through different channels carries different fulfillment conditions and penalties
Kestrel & Pine's marketplace and wholesale revenue, with hand-keyed orders living only in the ERP
Orders created by outside systems, and the part's running jacket examples
Core decision: every order authoritative in the order record, connectors translate while owners keep promises
Marketplace chapter preview: listings, stock sync, penalties, connector ownership
B2B chapter preview: company accounts, terms and credit limits gating order acceptance
EDI and e-invoicing chapter preview: shipment notices matching packed goods, mandates
ERP chapter preview: ERP's financial role and faster stock route than batches
Problems trace to orders or promises from the wrong place; start with marketplaces

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All nine aligned summaries carry the controlling idea of their spec paragraph (p01 to p09) in the declared order; the callout is p04's evidence and has no own paragraph. Small drift: the p08 summary omits the ERP partner's connector case.
Marked two_ideas, but it is the KEY POINTS callout whose house shape requires three points; not a failure.

Marked two_ideas, but the spec's p03 controlling idea is one idea (someone else's system creates the order) illustrated by the part's routes; the examples are instances of the contrast, not a second claim.

Every unit traces to the supporting claims: ¶1 to P5-4, ¶2 to P5-1/P5-5 (keyed orders outside the order record), ¶3 to P5-2, ¶4 to P5-1 to P5-3, the chapter paragraphs to the claims their spec lists, and the closing to P5-1/P5-3.

The ¶2 statistics are followed by 'Keyed orders exist only in the ERP, outside the order record'; the ¶3 scenario by 'All share the warehouse and books of Eva's order'; each chapter case by a 'shows why'/'illustrates' sentence; the figures' captions state what they show (readers quote them). See the flow result on Figures 2 and 3 for their density.
Elaboration: naming 'Kestrel & Pine, the fictional outdoor brand' right after the opening's merchant makes it that merchant; implicit (no linking phrase) but both flow readers followed it.
Contrast expressed by 'Unlike in Parts II to IV, someone else's system creates the order'.
Cause-effect sentence: 'The keyed orders and the opening's penalties come from one decision'.
Elaboration at end of previous: 'The chapters take marketplaces, business buyers, trading-partner documents, then the ERP.'
Contrast: 'turns from consumers to companies'.
Elaboration: 'For the largest buyers' narrows the wholesale channel.
Sequence: 'Last,'.
Conclusion summary: the opening sentence gathers the chapters' cases ('The stale stock, the credit hold and the deduction').

Both readers describe problem -> company -> decision -> chapter map -> start, matching large_to_small with the chapters in the announced prerequisite order; neither marks any section unclear. Stops at 'order record', 'Eva's order' and 'Parts II to IV' concern terms the declared audience already knows from Parts I to IV and are not counted against the draft.

results.quote: Connectors should translate channel requirements while preserving ownership of prices, stock and orders: each promise sent out (stock, price and credit, pallet contents, the invoice) comes from its owner.
results.finding: Both readers re-read ¶4: the 'one decision' sentence is abstract and the paragraph then switches from where orders are created to 'promise', a new term inside a parenthesis whose list does not match the ownership list before it, so the one decision reads as two (flow-A items 9-10).
results.corroborated_by: flow-B items 10-11: 'authoritative' is abstract and 'promise' appears for the first time as a term of art inside a parenthesis-heavy sentence, so the one decision seems to become two.

results.quote: each promise sent out (stock, price and credit, pallet contents, the invoice) comes from its owner.
results.finding: Figures 2 and 3 sit back to back with no prose between them, and their captions carry new points (strike, daily batches, events, every failure as a promise from the wrong system) the body has not made (flow-A item 11).
results.corroborated_by: flow-B items 12-13: Figure 2's caption says more than the paragraph it illustrates; Figures 2 and 3 back to back with dense captions, the second introducing 'strike'.

results.spec_locus: /introduction/paragraphs/3 (controlling_idea: 'KEY POINTS bullet 3 adds that availability never waits on the ERP')
results.quote: so availability must never wait on a scheduled finance-system update.
results.finding: The ERP-timing point is set up nowhere in the body: the bullet's clause jumps from outside parties to finance-system timing, and 'Finance can consume complete batches' in Chapters ¶4 arrives with no body sentence saying the ERP works in batches (flow-B item 6). The spec assigns the point to the callout only, after round 3 cut the body sentence.
results.corroborated_by: flow-A item 14: the body never says the ERP works in batches, so the contrast in 'Finance can consume complete batches while stock availability needs a faster route' arrives late.

results.quote: The part's examples are routes for the same jacket: two Amazon.de orders on 13 April 2027;
results.finding: The two Amazon.de orders and their date are announced as the part's examples but never used again on the page (flow-A item 7); flow-A item 6 also found 'someone else's system creates the order' clashes with the keyed orders of ¶2, which Kestrel & Pine's own staff create.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B item 14: the two Amazon.de orders announced as the example for this route are not tied to the marketplace chapter's incident.

results.quote: a retired connector interface leaves one channel outdated for two days.
results.finding: A new incident with no setup; readers could not tell what was retired or whether it is the Amazon.de story (flow-B item 14).
results.corroborated_by: flow-A item 12: 'retired connector interface' is vague; could not tell whether it means an API version the marketplace shut down.

results.quote: The ERP partner's connector, which took three weeks to understand, illustrates the cost of undocumented ownership.
results.finding: 'The ERP partner' is referred to with a definite article but never introduced, so the case arrives without setup (flow-A item 13).
results.corroborated_by: flow-B item 16: another new incident with no setup; 'the ERP partner' has not been mentioned.

results.finding: Terms readers flagged that the audience already knows (order record, connector, ERP, EDI, Eva's order, Parts II to IV, system of record behind 'authoritative') pass; does_not_know items are handled as the spec says: despatch advice glossed as shipment notices, e-invoicing mandates and seller performance only named; strike and chargeback glossed at first use. 'Technical contract' (flow-B only) is left to the chapter.

results.quote: Connectors and electronic document providers carry facts between owners
results.finding: 'Electronic document providers' and 'electronic trading-partner orders' are new names for EDI providers and EDI orders, used before ¶3 introduces 'electronic data interchange (EDI) provider'; the audience knows EDI but not these names, and nothing links them (flow-A item 17).
results.corroborated_by: flow-B items 18-19: 'electronic document providers' is presumably the EDI provider introduced later, but the names differ.

results.finding: The introduction opens on a puzzling scenario (the same jacket ending in penalties or deductions), not a placeholder, restated question, definition or book report.
The closing names the chapters' cases and their shared cause and gives a course of action; no 'in conclusion', new idea, bare thesis restatement or body evidence.

'The stale stock, the credit hold and the deduction began as orders outside the order record or promises from the wrong system' synthesizes across chapters, and 'Begin with' gives the action; the so-what (not more channels or tools) is implied rather than stated.

The closing names the cause of the penalties and deductions set up in p01 ('the deduction' echoes the chain's pallet-label deduction); the callback is implicit, as it does not name the opening's jacket.
The intro reader predicted the four chapters in the roadmap's order (marketplaces, business buyers, trading-partner documents/EDI, then the ERP), matching the roadmap promise kept in 'chapters'.
The cold reader named the four chapters' subjects in reading order; the finer chapter details in 'expected' sit in the chapter paragraphs, which this reader (introduction only) did not see.

The reader gives the outside parties' non-negotiated rules (scorecard and late-dispatch penalties, pallet labels and chargebacks) and the decision of where each order becomes authoritative, with connectors translating and each promise from its owner; omitting the mandates' legal dates is immaterial to the probe.
